headline: Saudi Construction's Tightest Constraint May Be People, Not Materials
deck: A 3.4 million-strong workforce that is 92 per cent expatriate, more than 200,000 unfilled skilled roles, and a training system being asked to close the gap.
excerpt: Saudi Arabia's construction workforce stood at roughly 3.4 million in the fourth quarter of 2025, about 92 per cent of it non-Saudi, with industry estimates putting unfilled skilled positions above 200,000. Against a market forecast to grow 6.2 per cent this year, the binding constraint on delivery is increasingly labour rather than material.
content:
There is a version of the Saudi construction story that is entirely about capacity: cement plants, steel mills, admixture lines, block machines, tower cranes. Big 5 Construct Saudi is a good place to see that version, and it is largely accurate. It is also incomplete, because the constraint that shows up most consistently in conversations across the exhibition floor is not a material at all. It is people.

The numbers are not marginal. GASTAT's fourth-quarter 2025 labour force survey puts Saudi Arabia's construction workforce at approximately 3.4 million, of whom around 92 per cent are non-Saudi. The nationality mix is concentrated: roughly 28 per cent Indian, 18 per cent Bangladeshi, 16 per cent Pakistani, 9 per cent Nepali and 8 per cent Egyptian, with Filipino, Sudanese and other Arab nationals making up most of the balance. That is a workforce assembled through international recruitment channels, and it turns over continuously.

Against that base, industry estimates put current unfilled skilled positions in the sector above 200,000, with specialist roles in project management, engineering and skilled trades staying open for three to six months on average. Forward projections in the same work put the shortfall at around 663,000 skilled workers by 2030 if nothing changes, with a corresponding drag on delivered revenue. Those forecasts should be read with the usual caution attached to any long-range manpower model, but the direction is not seriously disputed by anyone contracting in the Kingdom.

The demand side keeps adding to it. Saudi construction output is forecast to grow 6.2 per cent this year to about SAR 232.14 billion. The Saudi Contractors Authority recorded 18 awards worth more than SR 30.03 billion in May and 25 awards worth over SR 29.5 billion in June. Beyond the construction phase, a facilities management market estimated around $52 billion in 2026 is absorbing technicians of exactly the type the construction sector is competing for, and it will keep doing so for the operating life of every asset now being handed over.

Saudization is the policy response, and it is working unevenly by design. Nationalisation targets under the Nitaqat framework are met comfortably in white-collar, supervisory and health, safety and environment roles. They are met far less comfortably in the skilled trades, where the bulk of headcount sits and where the work is physically demanding, often remote and historically low status. The practical consequence is that a large share of trade headcount remains open to expatriate recruitment, which keeps the sector exposed to source-country labour markets, visa policy and wage competition from neighbouring Gulf states.

Closing that gap is a training problem before it is a recruitment problem, and it is the reason vocational providers now appear at a construction exhibition. Institutes licensed by the Technical and Vocational Training Corporation, ASAS Training among them, sit alongside manufacturers in the halls, and the qualifications they issue have moved into the compliance stack: safety certification for supervisors is a prequalification requirement on large packages, not a nice-to-have. The harder task is trade capability, where curricula have to keep pace with methods that have changed materially in a decade, including precast assembly and erection, modular installation sequencing, advanced non-destructive testing and the maintenance of connected plant.

Technology is the other response, and it is further along than it was. Contractor adoption of jobsite robotics has risen sharply this year, with survey evidence indicating that the proportion of contractors using robotics in some form more than doubled over the past year, and that the share running pilots on at least one site rose from around 12 per cent to roughly 32 per cent. The applications that work are the repetitive, physically punishing or hazardous ones: layout, rebar tying, material handling, structural inspection and site scanning. Automated rebar tying machines that work across a mat can tie well over a thousand intersections an hour against a few hundred for a skilled ironworker, compressing a tying sequence on a large deck from around a fortnight to under a week.

It would be a mistake to read that as a substitution story. Robotics reduces the labour requirement on specific scopes; it does not build the supervisory, technical and maintenance capability that a site still needs, and in several cases it raises the skill floor rather than lowering it. Somebody has to commission the machine, interpret its output, keep it running in 45-degree heat and take responsibility for the work it produced.

What the exhibition floor makes visible is that Saudi contractors and manufacturers are now buying against this constraint explicitly. Equipment is being specified for lower manpower dependency. Materials are being selected for fewer site operations and less rework. Facilities management contracts are being written around systems that reduce the number of technicians required to hold an estate together. The Kingdom's building programme has never been short of ambition or, lately, of domestic industrial capacity. What it is short of is qualified people, and that is a slower thing to manufacture.
author: Mo Qureshi
seoTitle: Saudi Construction's Constraint Is People, Not Material
seoDescription: A 3.4 million construction workforce that is 92% expatriate and more than 200,000 unfilled skilled roles are shaping what Saudi contractors buy and how they build.
